supplement.where: Supplementary Materials appended to the same PDF (PDF pp. 27-89, supp. pp. 1-63). Processed data, code, materials, and survey questionnaires at https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/YD94Z; preregistrations of the natural experiments at https://osf.io/yd94z/registrations (PDF pp. 26, 87).
supplement.holds: Table S9 (natural-experiment arm means, SDs, Welch t, df, Cohen's d with 95% CI; PDF p. 52), Table S6 (full unbalanced samples; PDF p. 46), Table S7 (pilot; PDF p. 49), Tables S10a-S13e (event-time, COVID-period, control-variable, and subgroup regressions with 95% CIs; PDF pp. 55-73), Tables S14a-c (correlations and association changes among the metrics; PDF pp. 77-79), Table S15 (mediation total, direct, and indirect effects on creativity ratings with bootstrap 95% CIs; PDF p. 85), Table S16 (Controlled Experiment 3 mixed-model coefficients with 95% CIs and random effects; PDF p. 89), Table S8 (which hypotheses were preregistered; PDF p. 50), and study methods. The recorded contrasts report confidence intervals rather than numerical standard errors.

paper_design_summary: Four preregistered natural experiments compare admissions essays submitted before and after ChatGPT's release, scoring word-level diversity, within-essay sentence diversity, document distinctness across essays, and automated creativity ratings (PDF pp. 28-33, 52, 85). Supporting analyses include an archival pilot, comparisons of human and model-written essays, and creativity-rater validation (PDF pp. 48-49, 75-84). Controlled Experiment 3 analyzed 203 students after exclusions: each supplied an original admissions essay and wrote a generation prompt followed by a revision prompt; researchers generated the AI essays after data collection, and no study randomly assigned people to AI or randomized the order of AI conditions (PDF pp. 86-89).

task.description: College admissions personal statement answering: 'Please submit a brief essay, either personal or creative, which you feel best describes you.' Mean length 622.03 words (SD = 55.23) across the 2019-2025 cycles (Table S4a, PDF p. 40).

outcomes.name: Word-level diversity (Divergent Semantic Integration, DSI)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: DSI: mean semantic distance between all word pairs within one essay, from bert-large-uncased (layers 6-7) word embeddings (PDF pp. 28-29; Table S1, PDF p. 31). DSI was validated as an automated creativity score for stories (rs = .73-.85 with expert ratings); this paper uses it as word-level (surface) semantic diversity within one text, not as a comparison across people. Scores standardized within institution and level on pooled cycles excluding 2023 (Fig. 1 caption). Robustness: full unbalanced sample d = 0.20 [0.18, 0.21] (Table S6, PDF p. 46); with controls (word count, sentence count, sex, race, ethnicity, international status, English at home) beta = 0.23 [0.21, 0.24] (Table S12a, PDF p. 64); COVID-period model beta = 0.17 [0.15, 0.18] (Table S11a, PDF p. 59); event-time models show an upward trend before ChatGPT (Table S10a, PDF p. 55; Fig. S2).

contrasts.reported: Post-ChatGPT 0.16 (0.98) vs Pre-ChatGPT -0.08 (1.00), standardized z, mean (SD); n = 23,760 post, 47,520 pre essays; Welch t = 30.43, df = 48291.34; Cohen's d = 0.24 [0.23, 0.26]; p < .001 (table note).
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 52 (supp. p. 26), Table S9; PDF p. 8, Fig. 1; PDF p. 7

outcomes.name: Sentence-level diversity (mean pairwise distance between sentence embeddings within an essay)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Mean pairwise cosine distance between sentence embeddings (SBERT all-MiniLM-L6-v2) within one essay (PDF p. 29; Table S1). The paper calls it local variation of ideas within each text, so it measures variety among one writer's own ideas (codebook: flexibility), not a comparison across people. Standardized within institution. Robustness: full sample d = -0.09 [-0.10, -0.07] (Table S6, PDF p. 46); with controls beta = -0.12 [-0.13, -0.10] (Table S12a, PDF p. 64); COVID-period model beta = -0.09 [-0.11, -0.07] (Table S11a, PDF p. 59); event-time 2024 beta = -0.09 [-0.12, -0.06] and 2025 beta = -0.10 [-0.13, -0.08] vs 2023 (Table S10a, PDF p. 55).

contrasts.locator: PDF p. 52 (supp. p. 26), Table S9; PDF p. 8, Fig. 1

outcomes.name: Document-level distinctness (minimum distance to the nearest other essay in the same cycle)
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: For each essay, the smallest cosine distance between its OpenAI text-embedding-3-large document embedding and those of all other essays in the same admissions cycle (Table S1; PDF pp. 29-31). Higher = more distinct from other applicants' essays. Standardized within institution. Robustness: full sample d = -0.16 [-0.18, -0.15] (Table S6, PDF p. 46); with controls beta = -0.16 [-0.18, -0.14] (Table S12a, PDF p. 64); COVID-period model beta = -0.15 [-0.17, -0.14] (Table S11a, PDF p. 59); event-time 2024 beta = -0.11 [-0.14, -0.09] and 2025 beta = -0.16 [-0.19, -0.14] vs 2023 (Table S10a, PDF p. 55); subgroup models Tables S13a and S13e.

contrasts.locator: PDF p. 52 (supp. p. 26), Table S9; PDF p. 8, Fig. 1

diversity_detail.metric: Document-level distinctness: minimum pairwise cosine distance to the nearest other essay (after Cox et al.); higher = more diverse, so no sign reversal
diversity_detail.computed_over: Each essay against all other essays in the same admissions cycle at the same institution (nearest neighbor); cycles balanced to 11,880 essays by random sampling because cohort size affects nearest-neighbor distances
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Welch's t-test on essay-level standardized scores (essays treated as independent); Cohen's d with 95% CI
diversity_detail.notes: Defined in Table S1 (PDF p. 31) and PDF pp. 29-30; balancing rationale on PDF p. 33.

studies.label: Controlled Experiment 3: each student's original essay vs GPT-4.1 revised and generated essays built from the student's prompts

assignment.what_was_assigned: Nothing was randomized. Every participant contributes three essays: (1) the admissions essay they had submitted when applying, (2) an AI-revised essay that GPT-4.1 produced from the original essay plus the participant's revision prompt, and (3) an AI-generated essay that GPT-4.1 produced from the participant's generation prompt. The supplement describes one sequence (generation prompt first, revision prompt second) and mentions no counterbalancing. eligibility.reason: For the PDF on file, no study meets all three criteria. Criterion 1 is not met: S1-S5 compare archival essays by admissions cycle relative to ChatGPT's release, without assigning people to AI (PDF pp. 32-33, 48). S9 uses each student's original essay and two AI essays generated by researchers after data collection; all participants wrote a generation prompt followed by a revision prompt, with no random assignment or randomized condition order (PDF pp. 86-88). S9 is coded ai_vs_human because the researchers produced the AI outputs; no participant received AI output during the procedure. S6 also compares researcher-generated AI essays with archived human essays (PDF p. 75), S7 validates raters without assigning writers to AI (PDF pp. 80-81), and S8 is model-only (PDF pp. 82-84). Criterion 2 is met through S9: 224 recruited, 5 incomplete or invalid responses and 16 attention-check failures excluded, 203 people analyzed (PDF p. 86); these are the same people across all conditions, not separate arm samples. Distinct applicant counts for S1-S5 are unreported; their essay totals are not people counts (PDF pp. 36-39, 48). Criterion 3 is met: semantic diversity and distinctness are computed on essay text, including the participants' original essays in S9 (PDF pp. 28-31, 88-89); natural-experiment creativity ratings are also scored on essays (PDF pp. 13-15, 85). The principal evidence is observational context. Version uncertainty is tracked separately.

one_line_finding: Across four universities, post-ChatGPT admissions essays had higher word-level diversity (Cohen's d 0.15 to 0.39) but lower sentence-level diversity (d -0.18 to -0.06) and lower document-level distinctness (d -0.15 to -0.07) than pre-ChatGPT essays (PDF p. 7, Table S9 on PDF p. 52), and GPT-4.1 essays made from 203 students' prompts were less distinct than the students' original essays (AI-revised diff = -0.98, AI-generated diff = -1.52, PDF p. 16 and Table S16 on PDF p. 89).
open_questions: Resolved at finalization: S9 is ai_vs_human. Participants wrote prompts in the described sequence; researchers generated the AI essays after data collection (PDF pp. 86-88). The alternative quasi_people label would not satisfy random assignment. No further material is needed to decide eligibility for this procedure.

S9 original essays: the main text says all were submitted prior to 2022 (PDF p. 16), but the supplement reports transitional and post-ChatGPT applicants (PDF p. 86). Authors would need to reconcile the essay dates and establish actual prior AI use; this affects baseline interpretation, not the absent random assignment.

S9 document-level distinctness: Table S1 defines comparisons within a cohort (PDF p. 31), but the S9 methods do not specify whether that cohort contains essays from the same condition or all conditions (PDF p. 88). Posted scoring code/data would settle the comparison pool; the outcome is scored on essays either way.

Distinct people in S1-S5: the source reports essays/applications, not unique applicants (PDF pp. 36-39, 48). An author-confirmed count of unique writers by study would settle criterion 2 for those studies; the paper-level count criterion is already met by S9's 203 people analyzed (PDF p. 86).

Primary-outcome status of natural-experiment creativity ratings: Table S8 marks the mediation hypothesis preregistered at RP, FP and SL, but exploratory at EP (PDF p. 50); this does not establish primary status. The OSF preregistration documents would settle the outcome hierarchy. These secondary results are preserved in notes under the 15-outcome limit; primary status does not affect eligibility.

Possible shared sample with c017 (Moon, Green, and Kushlev 2025, cited as ref. 4 on PDF p. 22) and unspecified within-paper overlaps: the PDF does not confirm cross-paper overlap, exact S6/S7 overlap with the natural-experiment analytic samples, or whether S9 originals occur in S1. Author clarification or sample identifiers would settle reuse; it does not change the reported designs or eligibility criteria.

Version identity and latest full text: no version/date is printed on the PDF, and the search record's later version has a different title. The latest full text and its revision history must be inspected before carrying this PDF's decision to that version. Added or changed studies could affect any of the three eligibility criteria; no later-version change is assumed here.

Sentence-level Welch-test sample sizes in S2 and S3: Table S9 gives overall corpus arm totals rather than outcome-specific analyzed counts (PDF p. 52), while Tables S4b-c report missing sentence scores (PDF pp. 41-42) and regression tables report smaller Ns (PDF pp. 60-61, 65-66). The exact Welch-test Ns require posted analysis data/code; n_units is null for these two outcomes. These are output counts and do not affect the people threshold or the eligibility decision.

Controlled Experiment 2 (S8) is model-only: weights of the three metrics in model creativity ratings did not change systematically across 0 to 128 reference essays (PDF pp. 82-84, Fig. S4).

The alternative reading is kept in open_questions; neither is core, because nothing was randomized.

open_items.item: S9 design class: settled as ai_vs_human from the researcher-generated AI outputs and fixed described prompt sequence (PDF pp. 86-88). Neither this nor the alternative quasi_people label supplies random assignment.

S9 original-essay dates and prior AI use: authors must reconcile the conflict between PDF pp. 16 and 86 and confirm the baseline's actual AI exposure. This affects interpretation; random assignment remains absent.

S9 document-distinctness comparison pool: posted scoring code/data must identify whether essays are compared within condition or across all conditions (PDF pp. 31, 88). The measure is scored on essay output in either case.

Distinct applicant counts for S1-S5: author-confirmed unique-writer totals would settle criterion 2 for those studies (PDF pp. 36-39, 48). This does not overturn core=no; paper-level criterion 2 is met independently by S9's 203 people analyzed (PDF p. 86).

Primary-outcome status of the natural-experiment creativity ratings: inspect the OSF preregistration documents referenced in Table S8 (PDF p. 50). The PDF establishes preregistration of some mediation hypotheses, but not their primary status; this affects extraction priority, not eligibility.

Cross-paper overlap with c017 and unspecified within-paper sample overlap: authors or sample identifiers must establish reuse (PDF pp. 22, 33, 75, 80, 86). This affects duplicate-sample handling, not the reported eligibility criteria.

Version identity and latest full text: inspect the later paper version and revision history before transferring this decision to it. Added or changed studies could affect criteria 1, 2 or 3. The final core=no decision applies to the PDF on file, whose exact version is unverified.

S2/S3 sentence-level Welch-test Ns: posted analysis data/code must resolve missing-score counts and give the exact output totals for Table S9 (PDF pp. 41-42, 52, 60-61, 65-66). n_units is null; these are essays, so the uncertainty does not alter the people threshold or random-assignment decision.
